title: Simulation or postselection universality for two-qubit interactions
formal: Does every fixed two-qubit Hamiltonian \(H\) satisfy the following dichotomy in the source’s circuit model: its computations are efficiently classically simulable, or they are universal for quantum computation under postselection? The system starts in a computational-basis state, uses only chosen-time applications of H or its inverse on ordered pairs of qubits, and is measured in the computational basis. H need not be commuting. The second branch was lost in the saved extraction; the general easy-branch accuracy and real-parameter conventions still need specification.
context:
The source asks for classical simulability or universality under postselection for every two-qubit interaction. The saved statement ended before the second alternative and obscured that the commuting case is already treated in the paper.

For commuting H, the paper proves that interactions generating entanglement from a computational-basis input cannot be weakly sampled with pointwise multiplicative error c<√2 unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its third level. Interactions that never generate such entanglement are described as simulable. This does not classify all noncommuting H.

The September 2017 thesis repeats the conjecture in Section 4.8 and distinguishes larger-register and encoded computational universality from controllability on two qubits.

The 2022 theorem relates universal analog Hamiltonian simulation to QMA-completeness under faithful reductions and closure of a Hamiltonian family. Those low-energy simulation conditions do not supply the basis-input sampling or postselection dichotomy for one fixed interaction.
why: Seeks a boundary between classically manageable quantum dynamics and postselection universality using only one fixed two-qubit interaction. The restriction to basis preparation and measurement makes computational power depend on more than ordinary unitary controllability.
status_note: Read the full conference model, simulation definition and two-page question, checked the author’s 2017 thesis and arXiv version history, and checked the later analog-simulation theorem’s scope. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no general resolution. The remaining conventions prevent this draft from being certified as one fully specified open proposition.

Its precise commuting hardness theorem uses pointwise multiplicative error c<√2, which does not fix the easy-branch convention for arbitrary H. In addition, the source quantifies over arbitrary fixed Hermitian H and polynomial-bit time descriptions without a general representation/precision convention for their real constants. A completed benchmark must fix these conventions while preserving the basis-input, restricted-gate and postselection model; this review does not choose a new dichotomy on the source’s behalf.

sentences: The proposed dichotomy covers every fixed two-qubit interaction, including noncommuting ones.
Circuits begin and end in the computational basis and have no freely supplied local gates.
The alternatives are efficient classical simulation or universality under postselection.
The source handles commuting interactions, while later analog Hamiltonian-universality results use a different model.
The general easy-branch accuracy and numerical representation still need specification before the statement is complete.

definitions:
A two-qubit Hamiltonian is a 4×4 Hermitian complex matrix H, fixed for an entire computational model rather than supplied as a growing input. A circuit may use polynomially many qubits, including ancillas initialized to known basis bits, and a polynomial-length sequence of gates \(e^{itH_{ij}}\), where i≠j is an ordered pair and t is a chosen real evolution time. Reversing the order of the pair applies the swapped interaction THT, with T exchanging |01⟩ and |10⟩. Negative times, equivalently exact access to −H, are allowed by the source. Other one-qubit gates, arbitrary local basis changes, arbitrary input states and intermediate adaptive measurements are not supplied for free.

A classical polynomial-time procedure, on the input bit string x, specifies the number of qubits, the basis input, the ordered sequence of pair applications and the time descriptions. The source requires polynomially many description bits and polynomially bounded time magnitudes. Since arbitrary H may not commute on overlapping pairs, the order and repetitions are part of a general circuit's description; the commuting special case may combine applications. Measuring all qubits in the computational basis yields a joint distribution P_x on bit strings. Constants in a putative simulation may depend on fixed H, but not arbitrarily on the input length.

Weak classical simulation means producing samples. For the source's precise multiplicative notion, a classical output distribution Q_x must satisfy \(P_x(z)/c\le Q_x(z)\le cP_x(z)\) for every x and output z. In particular, a zero-probability output must remain impossible. This differs from additive total-variation approximation, which bounds \(\frac12\sum_z|P_x(z)-Q_x(z)|\), and from strong simulation, which computes individual probabilities. Definition 2.2 and Theorem 2.3 specify a multiplicative hardness conclusion for commuting interactions; the general conjecture does not explicitly assign an accuracy quantifier or exact-sampling convention to its easy branch.

Postselection conditions the output on a specified nonzero-probability pattern of measurement outcomes, even if it occurs extremely rarely. It is not implemented by running the experiment until that event happens and charging that waiting time as polynomial. For language computation, the source specifies a designated decision bit and requires its conditional probability of being 1 to be at least 2/3 on yes inputs and at most 1/3 on no inputs. The postselection pattern is chosen uniformly in polynomial time; Definition 2.4 chooses it from the input length. Universality here means the ability to implement general postselected quantum computation with polynomial overhead, not just to produce one distribution with evidence of classical hardness.

A commuting H means that its copies on every pair commute, including opposite orientations and overlapping pairs. Equivalently the source requires [H⊗I,I⊗H]=[H⊗I,I⊗THT]=[H,THT]=0, with [A,B]=AB−BA. Its proved sampling dichotomy assumes this property. The general question removes it and allows computation on larger registers and encoded subspaces, so classifying which interactions generate every unitary on exactly two qubits is insufficient.

For a complete finite-computation statement, real constants in H and allowed evolution times need a representation and precision convention that supports uniform circuit generation and the selected simulator. The source's polynomial-bit wording alone does not specify that convention for arbitrary real H, especially in conjunction with exact or multiplicative simulation and rare postselection. This remains a formulation issue here, not a claimed negative solution based on noncomputable constants.
answer_criterion: After fixing the stated simulation-accuracy and numerical conventions, prove that every permitted fixed H has at least one of the two properties, or exhibit an H for which both fail, stating any assumptions. Generic universality, a classification only of commuting H, hardness of some output probabilities, or universality with free local gates does not settle the general dichotomy. The polynomial-hierarchy-collapse consequence of suitable postselection universality is conditional; it is not an unconditional classical lower bound.
